text: I'll start by looking at the workspace layout and the tax code.

The bug is clear: `round()` uses banker's rounding (round-half-to-even) on floats. $10.00 × 0.0725 = 0.725, which in binary floating point is slightly below or exactly at the half, and Python rounds it to 0.72 (even), while the expected half-up result is 0.73. Half-cent boundaries are exactly the "particular kind of boundary" finance described. Let me check the tests for expectations before changing it.

The tests confirm the intended behavior is round-half-up. I'll switch to `Decimal` arithmetic with `ROUND_HALF_UP`, converting via `str()` so the float's binary representation doesn't corrupt the half-cent value.

args.summary:
Root cause: `calculate_tax` in library/tax.py used Python's built-in `round()`, which applies banker's rounding (round-half-to-even) on floats. Amounts whose tax lands exactly on a half cent (e.g. $10.00 * 7.25% = 0.725) were rounded down to the even cent (0.72) instead of up to 0.73. This explains why the error always went in the customer's favor and only hit boundary amounts.

Fix: compute the tax with `Decimal` (built from `str()` of the inputs to avoid binary-float artifacts) and quantize to cents with `ROUND_HALF_UP`, matching the intended behavior asserted in tests/test_tax.py. `total_with_tax` builds on `calculate_tax`, so it is corrected too. The full test suite passes (29/29). No test files were modified.
